The Phillips Curve is an empirical relationship named after economist A.W. Phillips, showing an inverse trade-off between the rate of unemployment and the rate of wage inflation, or price inflation. Widely adopted as a guide for monetary policy in the nineteen-sixties, it collapsed in the nineteen-seventies, reshaping economic theory and practice. A.W. Phillips, in nineteen fifty-eight, observed data from the UK spanning from eighteen sixty-one to nineteen fifty-seven, showing that lower unemployment correlated with higher wage inflation. The curve slopes downward, reflecting this inverse relationship. It suggested to policymakers that they could choose a point on the curve: accept higher inflation to achieve lower unemployment, or tolerate more unemployment to keep inflation down. The curve became a cornerstone of Keynesian macroeconomic management in the nineteen-sixties, and many governments tried to exploit the trade-off. However, it collapsed in the nineteen-seventies during stagflation—simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment—which the original Phillips Curve implied could not happen. Milton Friedman and others argued that inflation expectations shift the curve, so attempting to permanently lower unemployment below its natural rate only raises inflation. The curve's failure prompted a reckoning in macroeconomics: expectations matter, and monetary policy cannot persistently trade off inflation for output gains. The failure reshaped monetary-policy theory and practice. One variable on the curve's axes is inflation, whose unpredictable behavior in the nineteen-seventies exposed flaws in the relationship. The other variable is unemployment, and the idea of a stable trade-off was central to the Phillips Curve's appeal. Milton Friedman's critique and emphasis on expectations were vindicated by the nineteen-seventies stagflation. Keynesian theory, which informed the Phillips Curve's policy use, was undermined by its failure.
